questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Read a description of a place as evidence about the observer who wrote it
questions.stem: A beekeeper's logbook opens with the hive in the field like a grey box nobody had bothered to paint. Which judgement best describes what the description reveals?

options.text: It reveals a keeper whose standards have slipped, since an unpainted hive is a neglected hive.
options.misconception: reads a visual detail as evidence of negligence

options.text: It reveals an observer who reads even the hive's appearance as a comment on how things are run.
It reveals a factual recorder, since the writer reports only what the hive visibly is.
options.misconception: assumes plain description excludes interpretation

options.text: It reveals a writer with a taste for colour, since the comparison was chosen for its looks.
options.misconception: reduces the figure of speech to ornament

questions.explanation: The hive is compared to an unpainted box, which reads the appearance as a comment on the keeper's own standard of care. Neglect, mere reportage, and decoration each take the sentence for something it does not say.
questions.hint: Ask what the comparison is doing to the keeper.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a metaphor carries the reasoning in an argument
questions.stem: A beekeeper's logbook argues, 'A colony is not a machine, whatever the textbooks say; a machine does not decide to leave.' Explain what the metaphor is being used to argue.

answer.exemplar: The writer takes the machine comparison that runs through the manuals and turns it against itself. A machine has no intention and cannot choose, so the fact that a colony can swarm, and chooses where to settle, counts as evidence against the mechanical account rather than merely a difference of emphasis. The sentence therefore works as an argument: it takes a comparison the reader probably accepts and shows that it fails on one decisive case. Because the metaphor is the vehicle for the reasoning rather than decoration beside it, removing it would leave the claim without its proof.

questions.explanation: The writer uses the machine comparison to show that a colony's choices do not fit a mechanical account, so the metaphor carries the argument itself. Treating it as an aside or a figure of speech leaves the reasoning unsupported.
questions.hint: Ask what the comparison proves, not what it decorates.

options.misconception: reads a figure of speech as a literal claim about bee behaviour

options.text: It argues that the fighting is about the flower rather than about theft, since no theft is understood.
It is sarcastic, because the keeper clearly expects the colony to admire a decisive grip.
options.misconception: reads a serious maxim as mockery

questions.explanation: The claim that bees have no word for robbery lets the writer explain the persistence of the fighting as a matter of what the bees can think, which is the argument. Decoration, literal description, and sarcasm each remove the reasoning the sentence depends on.
questions.hint: Ask what the absence of a word is being used to explain.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Foreshadowing planted and paid off in a passage
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a later passage pays off an earlier planted detail
questions.stem: A passage in a beekeeper's logbook contains this exchange: in April, 'The hive was heavier than it should have been for the time of year.' In August, 'They had made enough honey for two winters, and I had to move a frame out to make room.' Explain what the second passage pays off.

answer.exemplar: The April note is the plant: it records weight that is out of season, and it does so without comment, so the reader has to hold it in mind. The August note is the payoff, because the surplus honey is exactly what the surplus weight promised, and the practical step of removing a frame shows the writer discovering the same fact from the other end. A payoff is not a repetition of the plant but its later consequence in the story's own terms, so the detail returns with new meaning attached. Without the April line the August line would be routine good news rather than a confirmation.

questions.explanation: The April weight is the plant and the August surplus is its later consequence, so the detail returns with meaning attached. A payoff repeats the plant; without the early note the later one would be ordinary good news.
questions.hint: Ask what the August note confirms that April promised.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: A symbol without a fixed meaning
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a recurring comparison accumulates meaning without definition
questions.stem: A beekeeper's logbook uses a wet stone as a recurring comparison for the keeper's hands at the end of a long day. Explain how a recurring comparison can carry meaning without a settled definition.

answer.exemplar: The comparison returns several times, and each time it does a similar piece of work: it places the keeper's hands against something cold, unremarkable, and beyond repair or attention. That repeated use builds an association in the reader without the log ever stating a definition of the stone or a single lesson it stands for. Meaning here is cumulative and slightly open, since the reader can feel the weight of the image without being able to reduce it to one proposition, and the log's silence on the point is deliberate rather than accidental. The writer also gains a way of saying something about endurance without announcing that this is what is being said.

questions.explanation: The repeated comparison builds an association around coldness and wear without defining what the stone stands for, so its meaning is cumulative rather than settled. The writer gains a way to mark endurance without announcing it as a lesson.
questions.hint: Ask what the repetition accumulates rather than states.

questions.learningObjective: Explain how a borrowed comparison is tested and used as evidence
questions.stem: One keeper's logbook compares a colony that has been handled roughly to a dog that has been shouted at, arguing that it is not damaged but simply unwilling. Explain how the comparison functions as evidence in this argument.

answer.exemplar: The writer borrows a comparison the reader is likely to accept and then tests it against a single decisive case. Machines have no intentions and cannot select, so a colony's choice to swarm and settle elsewhere does not fit the mechanical account; the comparison fails on its own terms and the writer has shown why. That makes the figure of speech the evidence rather than an ornament, because the argument's force depends on the reader accepting the comparison and then seeing it break. questions.explanation: The shortage of boxes is planted in July and the August crowding into the roof is exactly the consequence that shortage prepares, so the plant is paid off concretely. A delivery, a swarm, and a decision to sell each attach the plant to something it does not produce.
questions.hint: Ask what a crowded colony does when there is no room.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Foreshadowing planted and paid off in a passage
questions.learningObjective: Identify a plant and its payoff in a paired set of lines

stimulus.body: Two lines kept on the same page. March: I have put a sheet of newspaper over the queen excluder, and the bees are furious about it. June: The queen is in the box as she should be, and the bees have accepted the paper without a sound.

questions.stem: Two lines kept on the same page appear in the logbook extract printed here. Which judgement best describes the relationship between the lines?

options.text: The March line plants the accepted newspaper, and the June line pays it off with a calm outcome.
The June line plants the method, and the March line shows that it had already been used before.
options.misconception: reverses the direction of preparation

options.text: The two lines are opposites, since fury and calm cannot both describe the same treatment.
options.misconception: reads different outcomes as a contradiction

options.text: The March line is simply a joke about bees disliking newspaper, with no later significance.
options.misconception: removes the plant from any later use

questions.explanation: The fuss in March sets up the June calm, so the earlier line prepares the later outcome and the reader reads the acceptance as a change. Reversing the direction, calling the two contradictory, and treating the March line as a joke each deny the link the pairing makes.
questions.hint: Ask why the June calm is worth recording.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Compare two descriptions that rely on shared knowledge
questions.stem: Two hives are described in a beekeeper's logbook in ways that should be compared: one in the wrong field, where we all know it, and one in the old field, where we all know that too. Which claim holds up?

options.text: Both descriptions are self-contained statements of fact about two identical hives.
options.misconception: ignores the shared appeal to shared knowledge

options.text: The first shows the keeper regretting the move, while the second shows pride in the old position.
options.misconception: reads a settled fact as an open feeling

options.text: Both descriptions rely on a shared understanding the reader is not given, which is what the phrasing does.
The second is stronger, because a place held long enough becomes objectively the right place.
options.misconception: ranks one placement as objectively better

questions.explanation: Both entries end by appealing to what everyone knows, which means the writer is relying on an understanding the text never supplies to the reader. Calling them self-contained, reading a settled statement as regret, and treating longevity as objective merit each miss that shared appeal.
questions.hint: Ask what we all know is doing in each line.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Identify the claim a paired comparison establishes
questions.stem: One keeper's logbook claims that patience is the only tool that cannot be bought and the only one that cannot be lost. Which claim does the comparison support?

options.text: That patience holds a position no purchased equipment can, which the writer treats as decisive.
That tools are generally a poor investment and keepers should stop buying them.
options.misconception: generalises the comparison into an argument against tools

options.text: That patience must be trained like a skill, in the way a tool must be practised.
options.misconception: turns the comparison into a claim about training

options.text: That the writer has never owned a good tool, since nothing bought has served.
options.misconception: infers a personal history from a general remark

questions.explanation: The comparison sets patience against bought equipment and finds the one thing that cannot be acquired or lost, which is the claim it supports. A general argument against tools, a claim about training, and a personal history each add content the sentence does not contain.
questions.hint: Ask what the two halves of the sentence claim together.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a comparison reorganises the keeper's understanding
questions.stem: The logbook's own comparison, that a colony is a document and the bees are writing it whether the keeper reads it or not, is examined in this item. Explain how this comparison functions as an argument rather than as an illustration.

answer.exemplar: The comparison takes the colony's behaviour and treats it as writing, which is a claim about what the behaviour means rather than a picture of what it looks like. The writer presses the point: if the bees are writing, then the keeper's task is reading, and a keeper who merely manages boxes has never actually read the document. That is why the figure of speech is the hinge of the argument, because the practical advice on the following pages depends on the reader accepting the idea that the colony is producing meaning. As illustration it would be a pleasant image; as argument it reorganises what the keeper is doing.

questions.explanation: The writing comparison claims that the colony's behaviour produces meaning the keeper must read, which is what the practical advice depends on. As illustration it would be a pleasant image; as argument it reorganises the keeper's work.
questions.hint: Ask what the keeper is said to be reading.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Judge the effect of a repeated image joined without explanation
questions.stem: One whitewashed hive appears in a beekeeper's logbook, and six entries later another whitewashed hive appears across the field. Which reading of the repetition is best supported?

options.text: The second hive mirrors the first, so the pair sets up a scene the log will later explain.
options.misconception: assumes a promised explanation the log never gives

options.text: The repetition is careless, since the writer should have distinguished the two hives by name.
options.misconception: supposes an error where a choice may be intended

options.text: The repetition links the two hives without explaining the link, which is what the images do.
The second hive stands for the first's owner, since the log treats other keepers with suspicion.
options.misconception: decodes one hive into a person without support

questions.explanation: The repeated image connects two hives and the log never says why, which is the operation of an image that is not decoded. A promised explanation, carelessness, and a hidden person each supply a purpose the passage withholds.
questions.hint: Ask what the repetition connects and what it omits.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: A symbol without a fixed meaning
questions.learningObjective: Judge the function of a line set apart from practical lists

stimulus.body: The logbook's back pages are used for lists: frames to buy, jars to sterilise, fields to mow. On the same page, at the bottom, in a shakier hand, a single line: bees are quiet in rain. Nothing connects it to the lists.

questions.stem: On the back pages of a logbook extract, lists of frames and jars are followed by one shaky line. Which judgement best describes that last line?

options.text: It is a note from another keeper, wrongly copied into the keeper's own book.
options.misconception: invents a second author the entry does not suggest

options.text: It is a proverb, quoted to instruct a beginner reading the page.
options.misconception: supplies a source and a purpose the entry lacks

options.text: It is an error, since it belongs with the notes about rain and equipment.
options.misconception: corrects the line the log deliberately keeps

options.text: It is an image set apart from its surroundings, carrying weight the log never explains.

questions.explanation: The line is set apart from the practical lists and given no explanation, so it functions as an image rather than as a note, an instruction, or an error. That separation is exactly how a symbol works without a fixed meaning.
questions.hint: Ask why the line sits where it does.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Explain how an early defect prepares a later breakdown
questions.stem: One rattling extractor is planted in a beekeeper's logbook and paid off in another, and the two are compared here. Comparing the two, what holds up?

options.text: The first line is a plant and the second is a separate note, since a repair is not a story event.
options.misconception: denies that a practical repair can carry a payoff

options.text: The first line prepares the later breakage, and the repair cost is the consequence that makes it land.
The two lines show the keeper's finances rather than preparing anything for later.
options.misconception: reads the pairing as a theme without preparation

options.text: The second line overturns the first, since the writer had never intended to repair the machine.
options.misconception: treats a payoff as a contradiction

questions.explanation: The neglected rattle prepares the breakdown, and the repair cost is the specific consequence that gives the plant its force. A plant without a payoff, a financial theme, and a contradiction each misdescribe how the two entries relate.
questions.hint: Ask what the rattle was getting ready for.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Foreshadowing planted and paid off in a passage
questions.learningObjective: Explain how room provided earlier becomes space used later
questions.stem: An April entry about a low box under a high one is followed in a beekeeper's logbook by a June entry about the colony filling it. Which judgement best describes what the second passage does?

options.text: It repeats the April arrangement, confirming that the keeper's plan was carried out.
options.misconception: misses that the second passage shows growth rather than compliance

options.text: It pays off the April arrangement, since the extra room becomes the space the colony fills.
It contradicts the April arrangement, since a colony should never be left with a full box.
options.misconception: reads a healthy outcome as a contradiction

options.text: It plants a further problem, since a full low box can only lead to swarming later on.
options.misconception: treats a payoff as the start of another plant

questions.explanation: The room provided in April is the space the bees fill in June, so the later passage delivers the earlier arrangement's consequence. Repetition, contradiction, and a planted new problem each misdescribe the payoff.
questions.hint: Ask what the extra room is used for.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a comic comparison records the observer's way of coping
questions.stem: A beekeeper's logbook writes of a hive after a storm, the frames lying over like a crowd that had been told to sit down. Explain what the description shows about the writer.

answer.exemplar: The writer's comparison is a joke with a serious edge, since a crowd told to sit down is a crowd that has been told to sit down, and that is what the frames look like after the wind has flattened the colony's arrangements. The image is chosen for its comedy but it records a real disorder, and the writer's decision to find it funny rather than alarming tells the reader something about how the keeper copes with damage. Description in this entry is not neutral inventory; it is the place where the writer's manner of handling what has happened becomes visible. The mood of the page is a defence, and the comparison is the defence in operation.

questions.explanation: The comparison is comic in form and diagnostic in content, and choosing comedy over alarm shows the writer's way of handling damage. The description is where the keeper's coping becomes visible, not neutral inventory.
questions.hint: Ask why the writer chose comedy for this damage.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Identify the claim a comparison is used to establish
questions.stem: One keeper writes in a beekeeper's logbook that every hive has a temperament, in the way that a river has a temperament, since it will go where it always went. Which is the most accurate account of the comparison?

options.text: It argues that colonies have consistent characters, using the river to make the claim persuasive.
It argues that colonies are ungovernable, since rivers cannot be made to do anything else.
options.misconception: draws a stronger conclusion than the sentence supports

options.text: It decorates the claim, adding a familiar image to a plain statement about habit.
options.misconception: calls the comparison decorative when it carries the argument

options.text: It criticises other keepers, who treat every hive as though it behaved the same way.
options.misconception: makes the comparison an attack on unnamed keepers

questions.explanation: The river case is offered to establish that a colony has a consistent character, which is the argument the writer wants, and the comparison is what makes it persuasive. A stronger claim about ungovernability, decoration, and criticism of others each misread the sentence.
questions.hint: Ask what the river case is being used to prove.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Identify the claim a metaphor is being used to advance

stimulus.body: An argument written across two pages of the logbook: The frames are the argument. I set them, I space them, I say what the colony should be able to do between them, and the colony answers in honey or in nothing. This is not a tool I use; it is the argument I make.

questions.stem: An extract from a beekeeper's logbook argues that the frames are the argument. Which judgement best describes the work of the metaphor?

options.text: It shows that frame-setting is the most important task in keeping bees, above all others.
options.misconception: reads the figure as a ranking of practical tasks

options.text: It explains the physical spacing of frames and why spacing changes what a colony can do.
options.misconception: takes the figure as a technical explanation

options.text: It flatters the keeper, since it presents the writer as a careful student of the colony.
options.misconception: reads the figure as praise of the writer

options.text: It argues that the keeper's arrangements express a claim that the colony answers either way.

questions.explanation: The frames are made to stand for the keeper's claim on the colony, and the argument is that the colony will confirm or refute it, which is what the metaphor is for. A ranking of tasks, a technical explanation, and flattery each substitute a different claim.
questions.hint: Ask what the colony is being said to answer.

questions.topic: Foreshadowing planted and paid off in a passage
questions.learningObjective: Explain how an early observation makes a later entry legible
questions.stem: A May entry about dandelions is followed in a beekeeper's logbook by an August entry about what was still in the boxes. Comparing the passages, what holds up?

options.text: The May line plants a harvest and the August line merely repeats it in a different month.
options.misconception: reduces the payoff to a restatement of the plant

options.text: The May line prepares the August line, since the early flow is what makes the stored honey possible.
The two passages are unrelated, since the mention of dandelions in May does not affect August.
options.misconception: denies the link between the two entries

options.text: The August line overturns the May line, since early work rarely means a good year.
options.misconception: treats a consistent result as a reversal

questions.explanation: The early flow in May is what makes the stored honey possible in August, so the later passage delivers the consequence the earlier one set up. A restatement, unrelated entries, and a reversal each misdescribe the relationship.
questions.hint: Ask what the May flow has to do with August.
